<thought>
Excellent! When I added NH₃ (base) to the sample, a white precipitate formed. This is very diagnostic!

With Ca²⁺ and NH₃:
- If the anion is NO₃⁻: Ca(NO₃)₂ + NH₃ → No precipitate (both are soluble)
- If the anion is H₂PO₄⁻: Ca(H₂PO₄)₂ + NH₃ → The base converts H₂PO₄⁻ to HPO₄²⁻ or PO₄³⁻, which forms Ca₃(PO₄)₂ (white precipitate)

The white precipitate that formed when adding ammonia strongly suggests the anion is H₂PO₄⁻ (dihydrogen phosphate).

This makes sense with all observations:
1. No precipitate with AgNO₃ - phosphate doesn't precipitate with Ag⁺ in acidic conditions
2. No precipitate with Ba(NO₃)₂ - at pH 5, H₂PO₄⁻ doesn't readily precipitate with Ba²⁺
3. pH = 5 - consistent with Ca(H₂PO₄)₂ being acidic
4. White precipitate with NH₃ - base converts H₂PO₄⁻ to phosphate forms that precipitate with Ca²⁺ as Ca₃(PO₄)₂

The anion is H₂PO₄⁻ (dihydrogen phosphate).
</thought>
